title: The exponential wall
summary: Why simulating qubits gets out of hand, why noise is the real enemy, and what 'logical qubit' means.

shots.title:
The exponential
wall.
shots.subtitle: Each qubit doubles what a classical computer must track.
shots.narration: Why would anyone build a quantum computer? Because simulating one on a classical machine gets out of hand, fast.

shots.text: …nature isn't classical, dammit, and if you want to make a simulation of nature, you'd better make it quantum mechanical…
shots.narration: Richard Feynman made the argument in a paper published in 1982: to simulate quantum physics efficiently, you'd want a computer that itself runs on quantum rules.
Here's why. Describing n qubits takes two to the n amplitudes. Every qubit doubles the list. At fifty qubits, storing them naively needs about eighteen petabytes of memory.

shots.text: But brute force isn't the only way. Clever classical methods — **tensor networks** — can simulate some large circuits after all.
shots.narration: But careful. Brute force isn't the only classical method. Clever techniques called tensor networks can simulate some large circuits, which is why quantum speed claims keep getting challenged.

shots.text: The real enemy is **noise**. Qubits leak information to their surroundings; every gate adds a little error.
shots.narration: The real enemy is noise. Qubits leak information to their surroundings, and every gate adds a little error. Long algorithms drown in it.

shots.text: John Preskill called today's machines **NISQ**: noisy, intermediate-scale. Useful for experiments — not yet for long, exact algorithms.
shots.narration: In 2018 the physicist John Preskill gave this era a name: NISQ, noisy intermediate-scale quantum. Good for experiments, not yet for long, exact algorithms.
The fix is error correction: spread one reliable logical qubit across many noisy physical ones, constantly checking for errors. Serious finance algorithms are costed in logical qubits.

shots.text: When you read a qubit count, ask: **physical or logical?** The ratio depends on the hardware and the code — and it is never one to one.
shots.narration: So whenever you see a qubit count in a headline, ask one question: physical or logical? The gap between them is where most of the engineering, and most of the hype, lives.

questions.prompt: How many complex amplitudes describe a general state of 10 qubits?
A headline says a chip has 100 qubits. What should you ask first?
options: Nothing — more qubits always means more power
questions.explain: Large algorithms need error-corrected logical qubits, each built from many physical ones.

questions.prompt: Why do claims that a quantum computer did something 'impossible for classical computers' keep getting challenged?
options: Classical methods like tensor networks can sometimes simulate the task after all
questions.explain: In 2022, tensor networks reproduced Google's 2019 Sycamore task in about 15 hours on 512 GPUs.
